tasks.heading: 7. Public sources and nonclaims
tasks.title: V07/C07 — Capacity planning and cost/performance trade-offs
tasks.content:
## 7. Public sources and nonclaims

| Source reviewed | Supports | Not demonstrated |
|---|---|---|
| [AWS Well-Architected: Cost Optimization design principles](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/cost-dp.html) | Cost attribution, consumption, outcome efficiency and operation | Current provider pricing or a real bill |
| [AWS Well-Architected: Demand/supply resources](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/2024-06-27/framework/cost-mandem.html) | Workload-aligned supply, buffers/throttling, scaling-lag consideration | Economic viability of the invented options |
| [AWS Cost Based on Workload Metrics](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/cost_monitor_usage_allocate_outcome.html) | Output-based unit economics and allocation principles | Real cost-per-journey data |

All amounts, charts, load assumptions and architectural examples are original teaching models. They
are not measured prices or actual workloads. The proposed decisions have no independent
financial/operational reviewer, validated capacity curve or tool run; edition metadata is recorded.

tasks.heading: 1. Four valid starting points
tasks.title: Workload and runtime modernization comparisons
tasks.content:
## 1. Four valid starting points

| Entry | What is actually known? | First discriminating task | Premature answer to avoid |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Requirement** | A wanted outcome, not its implementation | Quantify workloads, user-visible quality targets, hard constraints, data ownership | Select microservices merely because future growth is mentioned |
| **Symptom** | An observed failure or service-level degradation, not necessarily root cause | Correlate offered/completed demand, latency, retries, queues and dependency state | Replace synchronous calls with Kafka because p99 increased |
| **Legacy constraint** | Existing runtime/data/API boundaries that cannot all change at once | Inventory versions, consumer compatibility, committed state and operational ownership | Recommend big-bang rewriting as a universal migration |
| **Modernization objective** | Desired reduction in risk or cost/change latency | Compare retain, in-place upgrade, branch-by-abstraction and extraction | Assume independent deployment is the goal itself |

A valid outcome may be **retain**, **stabilize first**, **measure first**, **conditional candidate**, **contraindicated** or **insufficient evidence**. An agent or reviewer should be able to trace each exclusion to a named hard requirement and a specific supporting source or experiment.

<!-- /tycho-question-source -->
<!-- tycho-question-source:tycho.page.0ce5d0aaf63f425ebf556ea97e2d24a9:2 -->

tasks.heading: Migration and validation
tasks.title: Uber — MySQL to MyRocks: storage engine economics under real workloads
tasks.content:
## Migration and validation

For a comparable project, pin query distribution and secondary-index assumptions, shadow representative read patterns, validate data consistency across snapshot and live writes, trial write/compaction backlog and staged failover, and retain a rollback before deleting the old representation. These are Tycho's recommended tests, not a reproduced Uber deployment script.

Suggested decision record for a different organization:

| Verification gate | Evidence needed before accepting change | Rollback or hold |
|---|---|---|
| Interface and ownership | Inventory of dependent clients, schema/contract/API compatibility and authorized owner | Preserve existing public contract |
| Representative workload | Actual traffic mix, failure modes and capacity baseline; no invented p99 | Roll back the cohort if its own SLO worsens |
| Correctness | Domain-specific business invariants, dual-state reconciliation if used, idempotent replays | Keep authoritative old representation until proven |
| Operability | Error budgets, runbooks, trace continuity, incident ownership and cost | Stop rollout without a clear incident response owner |

The gates in this table are Tycho's **analytical adaptation**, not an assertion that the source's engineers measured these same four things.

tasks.heading: DNS and discovery have different update boundaries
tasks.title: Discovery, load balancing and backend selection
tasks.content:
## DNS and discovery have different update boundaries

In a typical DNS path, a recursive resolver may answer from a cached record or consult the authoritative naming hierarchy. The application/runtime can also retain resolved addresses or established connections. A DNS TTL governs a DNS record's caching contract; it is not an application transaction deadline or a guarantee that every client stops using an existing connection at that instant.

Service discovery may publish addresses plus eligibility metadata to a proxy or client. Document who observes updates and how stale membership is detected. Distinguish the discovery control path from data-plane requests that can continue against a last-known usable set. If membership is stale, continued reachability still cannot establish write authority.

**Client-side discovery.** The caller obtains the membership view from a registry/control
plane, caches it and selects a backend. It owns client-side load balancing, health/ejection,
retry budget and stale-membership handling. Registry unavailability, stale cache and uneven
client logic are common; a last-known set may serve reads but cannot grant write authority.

**Server-side discovery.** A proxy, gateway or platform keeps the membership view and selects
a backend for a stable virtual name. The client carries no discovery logic, but the proxy
becomes a shared dependency and must expose routing/health behavior. It may be preferable
for thin or heterogeneous clients; client-side discovery may be preferable when callers need
direct routing or cannot share a proxy. Static DNS, a service mesh or direct endpoint
configuration may be simpler when membership changes are rare.

For an original cutover decision, publish the replacement endpoint, establish its readiness and trust, and account for old route/connection lifetimes before retiring the former endpoint. A DNS change alone is neither a drain procedure nor a database failover protocol. The exact resolver/runtime's cache and failure behavior remains a product-specific verification task.

tasks.heading: 1. The contract has multiple layers
tasks.title: API contracts and effect identity
tasks.content:
## 1. The contract has multiple layers

| Contract layer | The caller needs to know | Typical failure if omitted |
|---|---|---|
| Operation and effect | Read/query, command, creation, update, cancellation; what “success” commits | A timed-out creation is retried and duplicated |
| Identity and authorization | Principal, resource identity, object-level permissions, tenant/isolation boundary | Caller sees success for a resource it should not control |
| Schema | Required/optional fields, defaults, absent vs null, unknown fields, enum behavior | An older consumer misreads a new response |
| Transport and scheduling | Deadline, cancellation, retry budget, maximum message size, streaming | Caller times out while provider continues wasting resources |
| Failure envelope | Distinguishable validation, conflict, transient overload, unavailable, unknown outcome | Client retries a permanent violation or gives up on an applied command |
| Compatibility | Client/server versions coexisting, migration window, deprecation and recovery | A routine canary release breaks a still-active old client |

A code generator or OpenAPI document makes an interface machine-readable; neither proves business idempotency, authorization correctness, or successful mixed-version operation. OpenAPI Specification 3.2.1 describes HTTP API operations, parameters, payloads and responses. Its existence is a **contract artifact**, not measured conformance of runtime code.

<!-- /tycho-question-source -->
